title_en: Adjective endings after the definite article

rule.summary: An adjective directly in front of a noun always needs an ending. After the definite article (*der, die, das*) and the *der*-words (*dieser, jener, jeder, welcher, mancher*, plural *alle*), the article already shows case, gender and number, so the adjective takes the **weak** ending: only **-e** or **-en**. You need this in almost every noun phrase with a description: *der neue Chef, mit dem alten Auto, trotz des schlechten Wetters*.
rule.table:
| | maskulin | feminin | neutral | Plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nom | der nett**e** Mann | die nett**e** Frau | das nett**e** Kind | die nett**en** Kinder |
| Akk | den nett**en** Mann | die nett**e** Frau | das nett**e** Kind | die nett**en** Kinder |
| Dat | dem nett**en** Mann | der nett**en** Frau | dem nett**en** Kind | den nett**en** Kinder**n** |
| Gen | des nett**en** Mann**es** | der nett**en** Frau | des nett**en** Kind**es** | der nett**en** Kinder |
steps: Check the position: is the adjective directly before a noun? After *sein, werden, bleiben* it is predicative and has no ending (*Der Mann ist nett.*).
Find the gender and number of the noun (*der Tisch, die Lampe, das Bild, die Bilder*).
Find the case: the subject is Nominativ; the verb or the preposition decides Akkusativ, Dativ or Genitiv.
Singular Nominativ (m/f/n) or singular Akkusativ feminine/neuter → **-e**. Every other slot (masculine Akkusativ, all Dativ, all Genitiv, all plural forms) → **-en**.
Check the stem and the noun: *dunkel → dunkle, teuer → teure, hoch → hohe*; Dativ plural nouns add **-n** (*den Kindern*); masculine and neuter Genitiv nouns add **-(e)s** (*des Mannes*).
pitfalls: Strong endings after *der/das*: ✗ *das kleines Kind* → ✓ *das kleine Kind*. The endings *-er/-es* belong after *ein* or after no article (*ein kleines Kind*).
Masculine Akkusativ with *-e*: ✗ *Ich sehe den alte Mann.* → ✓ *Ich sehe den alten Mann.* Masculine is the only gender whose Akkusativ differs from the Nominativ.
Reading *die* as feminine singular when the noun is plural: ✗ *die große Fenster* → ✓ *die großen Fenster*. Every plural form takes *-en*.
Thinking *der* always means *-e*: ✗ *mit der neue Kollegin* → ✓ *mit der neuen Kollegin*. *der* is also feminine Dativ/Genitiv and plural Genitiv, and those slots take *-en*.
Adding an ending to a predicative adjective: ✗ *Das Essen ist kalte.* → ✓ *Das Essen ist kalt.*

items.en: The nice man lives next door.
items.explanation: *Der Mann* is the subject of *wohnt* → Nominativ. The masculine Nominativ article is **der**. After *der* the adjective is weak, and masculine Nominativ is one of the five **-e** slots: nett + -e → **nette**.

mistake.wrong: Der netter Mann wohnt nebenan.
mistake.why: *-er* is the ending after *ein* (*ein netter Mann*). After *der* the article already shows masculine Nominativ, so the adjective only takes *-e*.

examples.de: Der freundliche Busfahrer grüßt jeden Morgen.
examples.en: The friendly bus driver says hello every morning.

examples.de: Der rote Zug fährt gleich ab.
examples.en: The red train is about to leave.

items.en: The young woman is laughing.
items.explanation: *Die Frau* is the subject of *lacht* → Nominativ. *Frau* is feminine, so the article is **die**. Feminine Nominativ singular is an **-e** slot: jung + -e → **junge**.

mistake.wrong: Die jungen Frau lacht.
mistake.why: *die* + *-en* is the plural pattern (*die jungen Frauen*). With a singular feminine noun in the Nominativ the ending is *-e*.

examples.de: Die neue Nachbarin heißt Sara.
examples.en: The new neighbour is called Sara.

examples.de: Die kleine Bäckerei schließt um sechs.
examples.en: The small bakery closes at six.

items.en: The small child is sleeping.
items.explanation: *Das Kind* is the subject of *schläft* → Nominativ. *Kind* is neuter, so the article is **das**. Neuter Nominativ is an **-e** slot: klein + -e → **kleine**.

mistake.wrong: Das kleines Kind schläft.
mistake.why: *-es* is the strong neuter ending (*ein kleines Kind*). After *das* the article already carries the neuter signal, so the adjective takes only *-e*.

examples.de: Das alte Fenster ist kaputt.
examples.en: The old window is broken.

examples.de: Das neue Café ist bis Mitternacht geöffnet.
examples.en: The new café is open until midnight.

items.en: I know the nice man.
items.explanation: *kennen* takes an Akkusativ object, and *Mann* is masculine → article **den**. Masculine Akkusativ is not one of the five -e slots, so the weak ending is **-en**: nett + -en → **netten**.

mistake.wrong: Ich kenne den nette Mann.
mistake.why: *-e* is only for Nominativ m/f/n and Akkusativ f/n. When the article is *den* (masculine Akkusativ), the adjective always ends in *-en*.

examples.de: Ich frage den freundlichen Verkäufer.
examples.en: I'll ask the friendly salesman.

examples.de: Sie ruft den jungen Elektriker an.
examples.en: She is calling the young electrician.

items.en: She is buying the red bag.
items.explanation: *kaufen* takes an Akkusativ object. *Tasche* is feminine, and the feminine Akkusativ article is the same as the Nominativ: **die**. Feminine Akkusativ singular is an **-e** slot: rot + -e → **rote**.

mistake.wrong: Sie kauft die roten Tasche.
mistake.why: Many learners think Akkusativ always means *-en*. Only the masculine Akkusativ changes to *-en*; feminine Akkusativ keeps *-e*.

examples.de: Ich nehme die grüne Jacke.
examples.en: I'll take the green jacket.

examples.de: Er repariert die alte Lampe.
examples.en: He is repairing the old lamp.

items.en: He is reading the new book.
items.explanation: *das Buch* is the Akkusativ object of *lesen*. Neuter Akkusativ looks exactly like the Nominativ: article **das**, adjective **-e**: neu + -e → **neue**.

mistake.wrong: Er liest das neuen Buch.
mistake.why: The *-en* rule for the Akkusativ is only for masculine nouns. A neuter Akkusativ keeps the Nominativ form: *das neue Buch*.

examples.de: Wir mieten das kleine Ferienhaus am See.
examples.en: We are renting the small holiday house by the lake.

examples.de: Kannst du das offene Fenster schließen?
examples.en: Can you close the open window?

items.en: I'm helping the old man.
items.explanation: *helfen* always takes the Dativ → the old man is the Dativ object. The masculine Dativ article is **dem**. After *dem* the adjective is weak, and every Dativ slot takes **-en**: alt + -en → **alten**.

mistake.wrong: Ich helfe dem alte Mann.
mistake.why: After a definite article the Dativ never has *-e*. In all genders and in the plural the Dativ adjective ends in *-en*.

examples.de: Sie gibt dem kleinen Hund Wasser.
examples.en: She gives the little dog water.

examples.de: Wir schreiben dem neuen Vermieter eine E-Mail.
examples.en: We are writing an email to the new landlord.

items.en: We thank the kind teacher.
items.explanation: *danken* takes the Dativ (*jemandem danken*). *Lehrerin* is feminine, and the feminine Dativ article is **der**, not *die*. In the Dativ the weak ending is always **-en**: nett + -en → **netten**.

mistake.wrong: Wir danken der nette Lehrerin.
mistake.why: Learners see *der* and use the masculine Nominativ pattern *der nette*. Here *der* is feminine Dativ, so the adjective needs *-en*.

examples.de: Er antwortet der neuen Kundin sofort.
examples.en: He answers the new customer immediately.

examples.de: Wir gratulieren der jungen Mutter.
examples.en: We congratulate the young mother.

items.en: The car belongs to the rich man.
items.explanation: *gehören* names the owner in the Dativ (*jemandem gehören*). *Mann* is masculine → **dem**. *dem* already marks the Dativ, so the adjective is weak with **-en**: reich + -en → **reichen**.

mistake.wrong: Das Auto gehört dem reiche Mann.
mistake.why: *-e* never follows *dem*. The owner after *gehören* is Dativ, and a Dativ adjective after the article ends in *-en*.

examples.de: Das Fahrrad gehört dem jungen Briefträger.
examples.en: The bike belongs to the young postman.

examples.de: Die Wohnung gehört dem alten Ehepaar im Erdgeschoss.
examples.en: The flat belongs to the old couple on the ground floor.

items.en: The small children are playing outside.
items.explanation: *Kinder* is plural and the subject of *spielen* → Nominativ Plural, article **die**. In the plural the weak ending is **-en** in every case, also in the Nominativ: klein + -en → **kleinen**.

mistake.wrong: Die kleine Kinder spielen draußen.
mistake.why: *die* + *-e* is feminine singular. *Kinder* is plural, so the adjective must end in *-en*, even in the Nominativ.

examples.de: Die jungen Leute tanzen bis zum Morgen.
examples.en: The young people dance until morning.

examples.de: Die alten Bäume im Park sind über hundert Jahre alt.
examples.en: The old trees in the park are over a hundred years old.

items.en: I love this warm sweater.
items.explanation: *dieser* has the same endings as *der* (*diesen* = *den*), so the adjective after it is weak. *Pullover* is masculine and the Akkusativ object of *lieben* → **diesen**, and masculine Akkusativ takes **-en**: warm + -en → **warmen**.

mistake.wrong: Ich liebe diesen warme Pullover.
mistake.why: *dieser*-words work exactly like *der*. After *diesen* (masculine Akkusativ) the ending is *-en*, just as in *den warmen Pullover*.

examples.de: Kennst du diesen neuen Film?
examples.en: Do you know this new film?

examples.de: Ich finde diesen schwarzen Mantel elegant.
examples.en: I think this black coat is elegant.

items.en: He is drinking the cold beer.
items.explanation: *Bier* is neuter (*das Bier*) and the Akkusativ object of *trinken*. The neuter Akkusativ article stays **das**, and the adjective takes **-e**, as in the Nominativ: kalt + -e → **kalte**.

mistake.wrong: Er trinkt das kaltes Bier.
mistake.why: *-es* is the ending without an article (*Er trinkt kaltes Bier.*). With *das* in front, the adjective is weak and takes *-e*.

examples.de: Sie isst das warme Brötchen sofort.
examples.en: She eats the warm roll right away.

examples.de: Wir bestellen das vegetarische Menü.
examples.en: We'll order the vegetarian set menu.

items.en: I'm buying the new shirt.
items.explanation: *Hemd* is neuter (*das Hemd*), not masculine like English speakers often guess. It is the Akkusativ object of *kaufen*; neuter Akkusativ = Nominativ → **das** + **-e**: neu + -e → **neue**.

mistake.wrong: Ich kaufe den neuen Hemd.
mistake.why: *den neuen* is the masculine Akkusativ form. *Hemd* is neuter, so it stays *das neue Hemd*. Always check the gender of the noun first.

examples.de: Ich probiere das gestreifte Kleid an.
examples.en: I'm trying on the striped dress.

examples.de: Er bringt das kaputte Handy zur Reparatur.
examples.en: He is taking the broken phone in for repair.

items.en: We live in the big city.
items.explanation: *in* is a Wechselpräposition. *wohnen* answers the question *wo?* (location) → Dativ. *Stadt* is feminine, so the Dativ article is **der**, and every Dativ adjective takes **-en**: groß + -en → **großen**.

mistake.wrong: Wir wohnen in die große Stadt.
mistake.why: *in die große Stadt* is Akkusativ and means a direction (*Wir ziehen in die große Stadt.*). *wohnen* is a location, so *in* needs the Dativ: *in der großen Stadt*.

examples.de: Sie arbeitet in der neuen Klinik.
examples.en: She works at the new clinic.

examples.de: Das Geld liegt in der obersten Schublade.
examples.en: The money is in the top drawer.

items.en: The German wine is very good.
items.explanation: *Der Wein* is the subject → masculine Nominativ, an **-e** slot: deutsch + -e → **deutsche**. Adjectives of nationality are written in lower case in German. *gut* after *ist* is predicative and has no ending.

mistake.wrong: Der deutscher Wein ist sehr gut.
mistake.why: *-er* is the ending after *ein* or without an article (*ein deutscher Wein*, *deutscher Wein*). After *der* the adjective is weak: *der deutsche Wein* (lower case, unlike English *German*).

examples.de: Der italienische Kaffee ist stark.
examples.en: The Italian coffee is strong.

examples.de: Der französische Käse ist ziemlich teuer.
examples.en: The French cheese is quite expensive.

items.en: I'm meeting the young student.
items.explanation: *treffen* takes an Akkusativ object; *Student* is masculine → **den**, and the adjective takes **-en**: jung + -en → **jungen**. *Student* is also an n-Deklination noun, so the noun itself gets *-en* outside the Nominativ singular: *den jungen Studenten*.

mistake.wrong: Ich treffe den jungen Student.
mistake.why: The adjective is correct, but *Student* belongs to the n-Deklination: Akkusativ, Dativ and Genitiv singular are *Studenten*.

examples.de: Wir fragen den neuen Praktikanten.
examples.en: We'll ask the new intern.

examples.de: Kennst du den netten Kollegen von Anna?
examples.en: Do you know Anna's nice colleague?

items.en: The new shoes are very expensive.
items.explanation: *Schuhe* is the plural of *der Schuh* and the subject → Nominativ Plural, article **die**. All plural forms after a definite article take **-en**: neu + -en → **neuen**. *teuer* after *sind* is predicative and has no ending.

mistake.wrong: Die neue Schuhe sind sehr teuer.
mistake.why: Learners hear *die* and use the feminine singular ending *-e*. Check the noun: *Schuhe* is plural, and the verb *sind* is plural too, so the ending is *-en*.

examples.de: Die bunten Socken liegen im Schrank.
examples.en: The colourful socks are in the wardrobe.

examples.de: Die leeren Flaschen kommen in den Keller.
examples.en: The empty bottles go in the basement.

items.en: We help the old people.
items.explanation: *helfen* takes the Dativ. *Leute* exists only in the plural → Dativ Plural article **den**, adjective **-en** (alt + -en → **alten**), and the noun adds the Dativ-plural **-n**: *Leute → Leuten*.

mistake.wrong: Wir helfen den alten Leute.
mistake.why: In the Dativ plural the noun itself needs *-n* (unless the plural already ends in *-n* or *-s*): *den alten Leuten*.

examples.de: Die Lehrerin erklärt den neuen Schülern die Regeln.
examples.en: The teacher explains the rules to the new pupils.

examples.de: Wir zeigen den ausländischen Gästen die Altstadt.
examples.en: We are showing the foreign guests the old town.

items.en: The long book is boring.
items.explanation: *Das Buch* is the subject → neuter Nominativ, an **-e** slot: lang + -e → **lange**. The second adjective, *langweilig*, stands after *ist*; it is predicative and takes no ending.
items.pattern: das + Adj-**e** + Nomen (Nom. n.) … ist + Adj (no ending)

mistake.wrong: Das lange Buch ist langweiliges.
mistake.why: Only the adjective in front of the noun is declined. After *sein* the adjective has no ending: *ist langweilig*.

examples.de: Das neue Programm ist kompliziert.
examples.en: The new program is complicated.

examples.de: Das dunkle Zimmer ist sehr ruhig.
examples.en: The dark room is very quiet.

items.en: She loves the fresh air.
items.explanation: *Luft* is feminine (*die Luft*) and the Akkusativ object of *lieben*. Feminine Akkusativ has the same form as the Nominativ: **die** + **-e** → frisch + -e → **frische**.

mistake.wrong: Sie liebt die frischen Luft.
mistake.why: *Luft* is singular here. *die* + *-en* would signal a plural noun; with a feminine singular noun in the Akkusativ the ending stays *-e*.

examples.de: Wir genießen die warme Sonne.
examples.en: We're enjoying the warm sun.

examples.de: Er mag die ruhige Ecke in der Bibliothek.
examples.en: He likes the quiet corner in the library.

items.en: The new colleague is from Poland.
items.explanation: *Der Kollege* is the subject → masculine Nominativ → **-e**: neu + -e → **neue**. *Kollege* is an n-Deklination noun, but in the Nominativ singular neither the noun nor the adjective takes *-en*: *der neue Kollege*, but *den/dem/des neuen Kollegen*.

mistake.wrong: Der neuen Kollegen kommt aus Polen.
mistake.why: The n-Deklination *-en* appears only outside the Nominativ singular. As the subject, it is *der neue Kollege*.

examples.de: Der junge Praktikant spricht drei Sprachen.
examples.en: The young intern speaks three languages.

examples.de: Der freundliche Nachbar hilft uns oft.
examples.en: The friendly neighbour often helps us.

items.en: The young doctor works nights.
items.explanation: *Ärztin* is the feminine form of *der Arzt*. The suffix *-in* always makes a noun feminine → **die Ärztin**. It is the subject, so feminine Nominativ → **-e**: jung + -e → **junge**.

mistake.wrong: Der junge Ärztin arbeitet nachts.
mistake.why: *der* belongs to *der Arzt*. Every noun ending in *-in* is feminine, so the article is *die*: *die junge Ärztin*.

examples.de: Die neue Pflegerin kommt aus Spanien.
examples.en: The new nurse is from Spain.

examples.de: Die nette Kellnerin bringt uns die Speisekarte.
examples.en: The nice waitress brings us the menu.

items.en: The little child is already asleep.
items.explanation: In the Nominativ singular all three genders take **-e** after the definite article: *der kleine Hund, die kleine Katze, das kleine Kind*. The article alone shows the gender. *Kind* is neuter and the subject → klein + -e → **kleine**.

mistake.wrong: Das klein Kind schläft schon.
mistake.why: An adjective directly in front of a noun always needs an ending. Only a predicative adjective has none: *Das Kind ist klein.*

examples.de: Das kleine Dorf liegt direkt am Meer.
examples.en: The small village is right by the sea.

examples.de: Das alte Rathaus steht mitten im Zentrum.
examples.en: The old town hall stands right in the centre.

items.en: I don't know the new boss.
items.explanation: Compare the Nominativ *der neue Chef* with the Akkusativ *den neuen Chef*. Masculine is the only gender where the Akkusativ differs from the Nominativ, and both parts change: der → **den**, -e → **-en**. *nicht* at the end negates the sentence and does not change the ending.

mistake.wrong: Ich kenne der neue Chef nicht.
mistake.why: *der neue Chef* is the Nominativ form. The boss is the Akkusativ object of *kennen* (the subject is *ich*), so it must be *den neuen Chef*.

examples.de: Hast du den neuen Fahrplan schon gesehen?
examples.en: Have you seen the new timetable yet?

examples.de: Ich finde den richtigen Schlüssel nicht.
examples.en: I can't find the right key.

items.en: We're talking about the current situation.
items.explanation: In *sprechen über* (to talk about) the preposition *über* always takes the Akkusativ. *Lage* is feminine → **die**, and feminine Akkusativ keeps **-e**, the same as the Nominativ: aktuell + -e → **aktuelle**.

mistake.wrong: Wir sprechen über der aktuellen Lage.
mistake.why: *über* is a Wechselpräposition, but in the meaning *about* (a topic) it always takes the Akkusativ, never the Dativ.

examples.de: Sie diskutieren über die neue Regel.
examples.en: They are discussing the new rule.

examples.de: Ich ärgere mich über die laute Musik.
examples.en: I'm annoyed about the loud music.

items.en: He's sitting on the old chair.
items.explanation: *sitzen* describes a position (*wo?*), so the Wechselpräposition *auf* takes the Dativ. *Stuhl* is masculine → **dem**, and every Dativ adjective takes **-en**: alt + -en → **alten**. With movement it would be Akkusativ: *Er setzt sich auf den alten Stuhl* (also *-en*, because it is masculine Akkusativ).

mistake.wrong: Er sitzt auf den alten Stuhl.
mistake.why: *auf den* (Akkusativ) is for a direction, e.g. with *sich setzen*. *sitzen* is a location, so it needs the Dativ article *dem*.

examples.de: Die Katze schläft auf dem warmen Teppich.
examples.en: The cat is sleeping on the warm rug.

examples.de: Die Schlüssel liegen auf dem schwarzen Regal.
examples.en: The keys are on the black shelf.

items.en: The interesting books are up at the top.
items.explanation: *Bücher* is the plural of *das Buch* and the subject → Nominativ Plural, article **die**. After the definite article every plural adjective ends in **-en**: interessant + -en → **interessanten**.

mistake.wrong: Die interessante Bücher stehen oben.
mistake.why: The singular is *das interessante Buch* (-e), but the plural *die Bücher* needs *-en*. Do not keep the singular ending when the noun becomes plural.

examples.de: Die günstigen Zimmer sind leider schon weg.
examples.en: Unfortunately, the cheap rooms are already gone.

examples.de: Die wichtigen Dokumente liegen im Ordner.
examples.en: The important documents are in the folder.

items.en: I worked the whole weekend.
items.explanation: A time phrase without a preposition that answers *wie lange?* is in the Akkusativ. *Wochenende* is neuter (*das Wochenende*), so the Akkusativ is **das** + **-e**: ganz + -e → **ganze**. Compare masculine *den ganzen Tag* and feminine *die ganze Woche*.

mistake.wrong: Ich habe den ganzen Wochenende gearbeitet.
mistake.why: *den ganzen* is only for masculine nouns (*den ganzen Tag*). *Wochenende* is neuter: *das ganze Wochenende*.

examples.de: Er hat das ganze Semester nichts gelernt.
examples.en: He didn't learn anything the whole semester.

examples.de: Wir bleiben das ganze Jahr in Wien.
examples.en: We are staying in Vienna the whole year.

items.en: What was the first impression like?
items.explanation: Ordinal numbers (*erst-, zweit-, dritt-*) take the same endings as adjectives. *der Eindruck* is masculine and the subject of *war* → Nominativ → **-e**: erst- + -e → **erste**.

mistake.wrong: Wie war der erster Eindruck?
mistake.why: *-er* is the ending after *mein/ein* (*mein erster Eindruck*). After *der* the ordinal number is weak and takes *-e*.

examples.de: Der zweite Versuch war viel besser.
examples.en: The second attempt was much better.

examples.de: Der dritte Tag war am anstrengendsten.
examples.en: The third day was the most tiring.

items.de: Sie wohnt in der {{c1::dritten::drei → Ordinalzahl}} Etage.
items.en: She lives on the third floor.
items.explanation: *wohnen* is a location (*wo?*) → *in* + Dativ. *Etage* is feminine → Dativ **der**, and the ordinal takes the Dativ ending **-en**. The ordinal of *drei* is irregular: **dritt-** → **dritten**.

mistake.wrong: Sie wohnt in der dreiten Etage.
mistake.why: The ordinal of *drei* is irregular: *dritt-*. The other irregular ones are *erst-* (1), *siebt-* (7) and *acht-* (8).

examples.de: Das Büro ist in der vierten Etage.
examples.en: The office is on the fourth floor.

examples.de: Wir sitzen in der ersten Reihe.
examples.en: We are sitting in the first row.

items.en: We help the new students.
items.explanation: *helfen* takes the Dativ, and *Studenten* is plural here → Dativ Plural article **den**, adjective **-en**: neu + -en → **neuen**. The usual Dativ-plural *-n* is not added, because the plural *Studenten* already ends in *-n* (compare *den alten Leuten*).

mistake.wrong: Wir helfen den neue Studenten.
mistake.why: *den* here is Dativ Plural, and every plural and every Dativ form takes *-en* after the article: *den neuen Studenten*.

examples.de: Die Stadt hilft den kleinen Firmen.
examples.en: The city helps the small companies.

examples.de: Der Kellner bringt den hungrigen Touristen das Essen.
examples.en: The waiter brings the hungry tourists their food.

items.en: That's the best solution.
items.explanation: After *sein* the noun phrase is in the Nominativ: *die Lösung* is feminine. The superlative of *gut* is irregular: **best-**. In front of a noun with an article it takes the normal weak ending: feminine Nominativ → **-e** → **beste**.

mistake.wrong: Das ist die am besten Lösung.
mistake.why: *am besten* is only used without a noun (*Diese Lösung ist am besten.*). In front of a noun use the declined form: *die beste Lösung*.

examples.de: Das ist der schnellste Weg zum Bahnhof.
examples.en: That's the fastest way to the station.

examples.de: Sie ist die älteste Tochter der Familie.
examples.en: She is the oldest daughter in the family.

items.en: I'll take the cheaper flight.
items.explanation: The comparative *billiger* is built first; its *-er* is part of the stem, not a case ending. Then the weak ending follows: *nehmen* + Akkusativ, *Flug* is masculine → **den**, ending **-en**: billiger + -en → **billigeren**.

mistake.wrong: Ich nehme den billiger Flug.
mistake.why: The comparative *-er* does not replace the case ending. A comparative in front of a noun still needs its ending: billiger + -en → *den billigeren Flug*.

examples.de: Wir mieten den größeren Wagen.
examples.en: We're renting the bigger car.

examples.de: Sie wählt den kürzeren Weg.
examples.en: She chooses the shorter route.

items.de: Trotz des {{c1::schlechten::schlecht}} Wetters gehen wir raus.
items.en: Despite the bad weather, we're going out.
items.explanation: *trotz* takes the Genitiv (in writing and careful speech). *Wetter* is neuter → Genitiv **des Wetters**, with *-s* on the noun. After a definite article every Genitiv adjective ends in **-en**: schlecht + -en → **schlechten**.

mistake.wrong: Trotz des schlechte Wetters gehen wir raus.
mistake.why: *-e* never follows *des*. The Genitiv belongs to the *-en* slots in all genders and in the plural.

examples.de: Trotz des hohen Preises ist das Konzert ausverkauft.
examples.en: Despite the high price, the concert is sold out.

examples.de: Trotz des guten Essens war der Abend langweilig.
examples.en: Despite the good food, the evening was boring.

items.de: Die Ärztin gibt dem {{c1::kranken::krank}} Kind ein Medikament.
items.en: The doctor gives the sick child some medicine.
items.explanation: *geben* has two objects: the receiver in the Dativ and the thing in the Akkusativ (*ein Medikament*). *Kind* is neuter, and the neuter Dativ article is **dem**, the same as masculine. Dativ → **-en**: krank + -en → **kranken**.
items.pattern: geben + dem + Adj-**en** + Nomen (Dat. n.) + Akk.

mistake.wrong: Die Ärztin gibt das kranke Kind ein Medikament.
mistake.why: The person who receives something after *geben* is in the Dativ, not the Akkusativ. Neuter Dativ is *dem* + *-en*: *dem kranken Kind*.

examples.de: Wir zeigen dem neuen Team das Büro.
examples.en: We are showing the new team the office.

examples.de: Sie bringt dem kleinen Mädchen ein Glas Milch.
examples.en: She brings the little girl a glass of milk.

items.de: Kannst du bitte die {{c1::schmutzigen::schmutzig}} Teller spülen?
items.en: Can you wash the dirty plates, please?
items.explanation: *der Teller* has the same form in the plural: *die Teller*. Here the article **die** shows the plural, because a masculine singular Akkusativ would be *den Teller*. Plural → **-en**: schmutzig + -en → **schmutzigen**.

mistake.wrong: Kannst du bitte die schmutzige Teller spülen?
mistake.why: *Teller* is masculine, so *die* cannot be feminine singular here; it is the plural article, and plural takes *-en*.

examples.de: Ich wasche die nassen Handtücher noch einmal.
examples.en: I'll wash the wet towels again.

examples.de: Hast du die frischen Brötchen gekauft?
examples.en: Did you buy the fresh rolls?

items.de: Am Ende der {{c1::langen::lang}} Reise waren alle müde.
items.en: At the end of the long journey, everyone was tired.
items.explanation: *der langen Reise* says whose end it is → Genitiv attribute. The feminine Genitiv article is **der** (the same as the Dativ), and the feminine noun gets no Genitiv *-s*. Every Genitiv adjective after the article takes **-en**: lang + -en → **langen**.

mistake.wrong: Am Ende der lange Reise waren alle müde.
mistake.why: *der* + *-e* is only masculine Nominativ. Here *der* is feminine Genitiv, so the adjective needs *-en*.

examples.de: Der Preis der kleinen Wohnung ist fair.
examples.en: The price of the small flat is fair.

examples.de: Die Tür der alten Kirche ist offen.
examples.en: The door of the old church is open.

items.de: Die Eltern der {{c1::neuen::neu}} Schüler treffen sich heute Abend.
items.en: The parents of the new pupils are meeting this evening.
items.explanation: *der neuen Schüler* tells us whose parents → Genitiv. *Schüler* is plural here, and the Genitiv Plural article is **der**. Plural always takes **-en**: neu + -en → **neuen**. The plural noun gets no extra Genitiv ending.

mistake.wrong: Die Eltern der neue Schüler treffen sich heute Abend.
mistake.why: Learners read *der Schüler* as masculine Nominativ singular and use *-e*. Here it is Genitiv Plural, so the adjective ends in *-en*.

examples.de: Die Namen der erfolgreichen Teilnehmer stehen online.
examples.en: The names of the successful participants are online.

examples.de: Die Zimmer der kleinen Kinder sind oben.
examples.en: The small children's rooms are upstairs.

items.en: Every new employee gets a laptop.
items.explanation: *jeder* has the same endings as *der* (*jeder – der, jeden – den, jedem – dem*), so the adjective after it is weak. *Mitarbeiter* is masculine and the subject → Nominativ → **-e**: neu + -e → **neue**.

mistake.wrong: Jeder neuer Mitarbeiter bekommt einen Laptop.
mistake.why: The *-er* signal is already on *jeder*. The adjective does not repeat it; it takes the weak ending *-e*.

examples.de: Jede kleine Spende hilft.
examples.en: Every small donation helps.

examples.de: Jedes neue Mitglied zahlt im ersten Monat nichts.
examples.en: Every new member pays nothing in the first month.

items.en: Which grey coat do you mean?
items.explanation: *welcher* is a *der*-word: *welchen* = *den*. The subject is *du*, and *Mantel* is the masculine Akkusativ object of *meinen* → **welchen**. After it the adjective is weak with **-en**: grau + -en → **grauen**.

mistake.wrong: Welcher graue Mantel meinst du?
mistake.why: *welcher graue* is Nominativ. In this question *du* is the subject and the coat is the object of *meinen*, so it must be Akkusativ: *welchen grauen Mantel*.

examples.de: Welchen alten Film willst du heute Abend sehen?
examples.en: Which old film do you want to watch tonight?

examples.de: Welchen neuen Laptop empfehlen Sie?
examples.en: Which new laptop do you recommend?

items.en: All the new flats have a balcony.
items.explanation: *alle* works like the plural article *die*: it already shows the plural, so the adjective after it is weak. *Wohnungen* is the plural subject → **-en**: neu + -en → **neuen**.

mistake.wrong: Alle neue Wohnungen haben einen Balkon.
mistake.why: The plural ending *-e* belongs to phrases without a *der*-word (*neue Wohnungen*, *viele neue Wohnungen*). After *alle* the adjective takes *-en*, as after *die*.

examples.de: Alle großen Supermärkte sind sonntags geschlossen.
examples.en: All the big supermarkets are closed on Sundays.

examples.de: Alle alten Fotos sind im Album.
examples.en: All the old photos are in the album.

items.de: Mit dieser {{c1::dunklen::dunkel}} Jacke siehst du elegant aus.
items.en: You look elegant in this dark jacket.
items.focus: Dativ feminin · nach *mit dieser* · Adjektiv auf *-el*
items.explanation: *mit* always takes the Dativ. *Jacke* is feminine → Dativ **dieser**, and the weak Dativ ending is **-en**. Adjectives ending in *-el* drop the *e* of the stem when an ending is added: dunkel → dunkl- → **dunklen**.

mistake.wrong: Mit dieser dunkelen Jacke siehst du elegant aus.
mistake.why: With *-el* adjectives the stem *e* drops before any ending: *dunkel → dunklen*, not *dunkelen*.

examples.de: Mit dieser kleinen Kamera mache ich alle Fotos.
examples.en: I take all my photos with this small camera.

examples.de: Mit dieser neuen Methode lernen wir schneller.
examples.en: With this new method we learn faster.

items.de: Das {{c1::teure::teuer}} Restaurant am Markt ist immer voll.
items.en: The expensive restaurant on the market square is always full.
items.explanation: *Das Restaurant* is the subject → neuter Nominativ → **-e**. *teuer* ends in *-er* after the diphthong *eu*, so the *e* of the stem drops when an ending is added: teuer → teur- → **teure** (like *sauer → saure*).

mistake.wrong: Das teures Restaurant am Markt ist immer voll.
mistake.why: *-es* is the ending after *ein* (*ein teures Restaurant*). After *das* the adjective is weak and only takes *-e*: *das teure Restaurant*.

examples.de: Das saure Bonbon schmeckt nach Zitrone.
examples.en: The sour sweet tastes of lemon.

examples.de: Das saubere Geschirr steht im Schrank.
examples.en: The clean dishes are in the cupboard.

items.de: Vom {{c1::hohen::hoch}} Turm hat man einen schönen Blick über die Stadt.
items.en: From the tall tower you have a beautiful view over the city.
items.explanation: *vom* = *von dem*, and *von* always takes the Dativ. *Turm* is masculine → **dem** → **-en**. *hoch* loses its *c* when an ending is added: hoch → hoh- → **hohen**. (*einen schönen Blick* is Akkusativ after *ein*, also *-en*.)
items.pattern: vom (= von dem) + Adj-**en** + Nomen (Dat. m.)

mistake.wrong: Vom hochen Turm hat man einen schönen Blick über die Stadt.
mistake.why: Before an ending *hoch* becomes *hoh-*: *der hohe Turm, vom hohen Turm*. The form *hoch* stays only without an ending (*Der Turm ist hoch.*).

examples.de: Im hohen Gras leben viele Insekten.
examples.en: Many insects live in the tall grass.

examples.de: Am hohen Zaun hängt ein Schild.
examples.en: A sign is hanging on the high fence.

items.de: Stell die Blumen bitte auf den kleinen {{c1::runden::rund}} Tisch.
items.en: Please put the flowers on the small round table.
items.explanation: *stellen* is a movement to a place (*wohin?*), so *auf* takes the Akkusativ. *Tisch* is masculine → **den** → **-en**. When two adjectives stand before the noun, both take the same weak ending: *den kleinen* **runden** *Tisch*.
items.pattern: auf + den + Adj-**en** + Adj-**en** + Nomen (Akk. m.)

mistake.wrong: Stell die Blumen bitte auf den kleinen runde Tisch.
mistake.why: Every adjective in front of the noun takes the same ending. After *den* both need *-en*: *den kleinen runden Tisch*.

examples.de: Leg die Zeitung auf den alten braunen Schrank.
examples.en: Put the newspaper on the old brown cupboard.

examples.de: Häng das Bild an die lange weiße Wand.
examples.en: Hang the picture on the long white wall.

items.de: Wegen des {{c1::starken::stark}} Regens fällt das Spiel aus.
items.en: Because of the heavy rain, the match is cancelled.
items.explanation: *wegen* takes the Genitiv in standard written German. *der Regen* is masculine → **des Regens**: the article becomes *des* and the noun adds *-s*. Every Genitiv adjective after the article takes **-en**: stark + -en → **starken**.

mistake.wrong: Wegen des starken Regen fällt das Spiel aus.
mistake.why: The adjective is correct, but masculine and neuter nouns need the Genitiv *-(e)s*: *des starken Regens*. (In everyday speech you also hear *wegen dem starken Regen*, but the Genitiv is the standard form.)

examples.de: Wegen des dichten Verkehrs kommen wir zu spät.
examples.en: Because of the heavy traffic, we'll be late.

examples.de: Während des langen Fluges hat sie geschlafen.
examples.en: She slept during the long flight.

drills.instruction: Answer the question about the weak adjective endings.
drills.prompt: After a definite article, in which five slots does the adjective end in -e?
drills.answer: **Nominativ Singular** m/f/n (*der/die/das* nett**e**) and **Akkusativ Singular** f/n (*die/das* nett**e**). All other slots take **-en**.
drills.explanation: The weak declension has only two endings. A quick test: singular noun and Nominativ → *-e*; singular feminine or neuter noun in the Akkusativ → *-e*. Masculine Akkusativ, every Dativ, every Genitiv and every plural form → *-en*.

examples.de: Die alte Brücke ist gesperrt.
examples.en: The old bridge is closed.

examples.de: Auf der alten Brücke fahren keine Autos.
examples.en: No cars drive on the old bridge.

drills.instruction: Answer the question about the words that trigger the weak ending.
drills.prompt: Besides der/die/das, which words are followed by the same weak adjective endings?
drills.answer: The *der*-words: **dieser, jener, jeder, welcher, mancher** and, in the plural, **alle**.
drills.explanation: These words have the same endings as the definite article (dies**er** – d**er**, dies**en** – d**en**, dies**em** – d**em**). Because they already show case, gender and number, the adjective only needs *-e* or *-en*. *jeder* has no plural; in the plural you use *alle*.

examples.de: Jeden zweiten Montag habe ich frei.
examples.en: I have every second Monday off.

examples.de: Welche neuen Regeln gelten ab Januar?
examples.en: Which new rules apply from January?

drills.instruction: Explain the contrast between the two article types.
drills.prompt: Why do we say *der nette Mann* but *ein netter Mann*, and *das kleine Kind* but *ein kleines Kind*?
drills.answer: The case and gender signal must appear once. *der* and *das* show it themselves, so the adjective is weak (**-e/-en**). *ein* has no ending in Nominativ m and Nominativ/Akkusativ n, so the adjective must show it: nett**er**, klein**es**.
drills.explanation: German marks case and gender clearly on one word in the noun phrase. If the article carries the strong signal (*-r, -s, -m, -n*), the adjective takes the weak ending. If the article has no ending, the adjective carries the signal instead (mixed declension, topic *Adjektive nach unbestimmtem Artikel*).

examples.de: Das rote Auto gehört Lisa.
examples.en: The red car belongs to Lisa.

examples.de: Lisa fährt ein rotes Auto.
examples.en: Lisa drives a red car.

drills.instruction: Answer the question about adjectives without an ending.
drills.prompt: When does an adjective have no ending at all?
drills.answer: When it is not directly in front of a noun: after *sein, werden, bleiben* (predicative: *Die Prüfung war schwer.*) and when it is used as an adverb (*Sie singt schön.*). Only an adjective before a noun is declined.
drills.explanation: The ending belongs to the noun phrase, not to the adjective itself. In *Die Prüfung war schwer* the adjective describes the subject through the verb and stays in its base form. In *die schwere Prüfung* it stands inside the noun phrase and needs the ending.

examples.de: Die Prüfung war schwer.
examples.en: The exam was difficult.

examples.de: Die schwere Prüfung ist endlich vorbei.
examples.en: The difficult exam is finally over.

drills.instruction: Answer the question about spelling changes in the adjective stem.
drills.prompt: What happens to the stems of *dunkel*, *teuer* and *hoch* when they take an ending?
drills.answer: *-el* adjectives drop the *e*: dunkel → **dunkl**e. *-er* after *au/eu* drops the *e*: teuer → **teur**e, sauer → **saur**e. *hoch* loses the *c*: hoch → **hoh**e.
drills.explanation: These changes make the word easier to pronounce. After a consonant, *-er* adjectives usually keep the *e* (*sauber → die saubere Küche*). The change also happens in the Dativ and Genitiv: *im dunklen Keller, die hohen Mieten*.

examples.de: Im dunklen Keller ist es kalt.
examples.en: It's cold in the dark cellar.

examples.de: Die hohen Mieten sind ein großes Problem.
examples.en: The high rents are a big problem.

drills.prompt: Wir übernachten im ___ Hotel am Bahnhof.
drills.answer: Wir übernachten im günstigen Hotel am Bahnhof.
drills.explanation: *im* = *in dem*; *übernachten* is a location (*wo?*), so *in* takes the Dativ. Neuter Dativ after *dem* → *-en*. *günstige* is only for Nominativ or Akkusativ f/n singular, and *günstiges* is the ending after *ein* or without an article.

drills.prompt: Die ___ Nachbarin hat uns einen Kuchen gebracht.
drills.answer: Die freundliche Nachbarin hat uns einen Kuchen gebracht.
drills.explanation: *Nachbarin* is feminine singular and the subject → Nominativ → *-e*. *freundlichen* would need a plural noun (*die freundlichen Nachbarinnen*) or a Dativ/Genitiv. *freundlicher* is the ending after *ein* for masculine nouns (*ein freundlicher Nachbar*).

drills.prompt: Die Farbe des ___ Autos gefällt mir nicht.
drills.answer: Die Farbe des neuen Autos gefällt mir nicht.
drills.explanation: *des Autos* is a neuter Genitiv (whose colour?). Every Genitiv adjective after the definite article ends in *-en*. *neue* fits only Nominativ/Akkusativ singular, and *neues* is used after *ein* or without an article.

drills.prompt: Wir warten auf den letzte Bus.
drills.answer: Wir warten auf den letzten Bus.
drills.explanation: *warten auf* takes the Akkusativ, and *Bus* is masculine → *den*. Masculine Akkusativ is an *-en* slot, so *letzte* must be *letzten*.

drills.prompt: Ich gebe der neue Praktikantin den Schlüssel.
drills.answer: Ich gebe der neuen Praktikantin den Schlüssel.
drills.explanation: The receiver after *geben* is in the Dativ, and *Praktikantin* is feminine → *der*. Here *der* is feminine Dativ, not masculine Nominativ, so the adjective needs *-en*: *der neuen Praktikantin*.

drills.prompt: Die alte Häuser in der Altstadt sind schön.
drills.answer: Die alten Häuser in der Altstadt sind schön.
drills.explanation: *Häuser* is the plural of *das Haus*, and *die* is the plural article here. Every plural adjective after a definite article ends in *-en*: *die alten Häuser*.

drills.prompt: Der Kaffee ist heute sehr heiße.
drills.answer: Der Kaffee ist heute sehr heiß.
drills.explanation: *heiß* stands after *ist* and is predicative, so it takes no ending. Only an adjective in front of the noun is declined: *der heiße Kaffee*.

drills.instruction: Make the subject plural (*der Rucksack → die Rucksäcke*). Change the verb if needed.
drills.explanation: In the plural the Nominativ article is *die*, and every plural adjective takes *-en*: *rote → roten*. The noun gets its plural form with umlaut (*Rucksäcke*), and the verb agrees: *gehört → gehören*.

drills.instruction: Replace *die Mappe* with *der Ordner*. Adjust the article and the adjective.
drills.explanation: *suchen* takes the Akkusativ. Feminine Akkusativ is *die* + *-e*, but *Ordner* is masculine, and masculine Akkusativ is *den* + *-en*: *den blauen Ordner*.

drills.instruction: Replace *kennen* with *vertrauen* (+ Dativ). Adjust the noun phrase.
drills.explanation: *vertrauen* takes a Dativ object, so the masculine article changes from *den* to *dem*. The adjective stays *jungen*, because both masculine Akkusativ and Dativ are *-en* slots. *Arzt* is not an n-Deklination noun, so the noun does not change.

drills.instruction: Put the parts in the correct order. Start with: Wir
drills.prompt: fahren / dem / nach Berlin / wir / Zug / mit / schnellen
drills.answer: Wir fahren mit dem schnellen Zug nach Berlin.
drills.explanation: The finite verb *fahren* is in position 2. *mit* takes the Dativ: *mit dem schnellen Zug* (masculine Dativ → *-en*). The way (*mit dem Zug*) comes before the place (*nach Berlin*), the neutral order. Other correct sentences: *Mit dem schnellen Zug fahren wir nach Berlin.* / *Nach Berlin fahren wir mit dem schnellen Zug.*

drills.instruction: Put the parts in order to make a yes/no question.
drills.prompt: gesehen / den / du / spannenden / Film / hast
drills.answer: Hast du den spannenden Film gesehen?
drills.explanation: In a yes/no question the finite verb *hast* comes first and the Partizip II *gesehen* goes to the end (Satzklammer). *Film* is masculine and the Akkusativ object → *den spannenden Film* with *-en*.

drills.instruction: Make one sentence: put the adjective from the first sentence in front of the noun in the second sentence.
drills.prompt: Die Tasche ist schwer. Ich trage die Tasche.
drills.explanation: In the first sentence *schwer* is predicative and has no ending. In front of the noun it needs one: *die Tasche* is the feminine Akkusativ object of *tragen*, an *-e* slot → *die schwere Tasche*.

drills.instruction: Make one sentence: put the description from the second sentence in front of the noun in the first sentence.
drills.prompt: Ich habe mit dem Kellner gesprochen. Der Kellner war sehr freundlich.
drills.answer: Ich habe mit dem sehr freundlichen Kellner gesprochen.
drills.explanation: *mit* takes the Dativ, and *Kellner* is masculine → *dem* + *-en*: *freundlichen*. *sehr* is an adverb and never takes an ending; it simply stands before the adjective.
